target_customer: Software engineering teams at enterprises that build on GraphQL, buying the commercial GraphOS platform on top of open source Apollo tools
problem: The company began as Meteor Development Group, helping developers build real time full stack JavaScript apps, and later focused on a GraphQL data layer that unifies APIs for client apps.
business_model: Open source core with commercial enterprise SaaS subscriptions (open core)

founders.name: Geoff Schmidt
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as founder and CEO.

founders.name: Matt DeBergalis
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page as founder and CTO. Spelled Debergalis on the YC page.

founders.name: Nick Martin
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page as founder and CTO.

competitors.name: Derby
competitors.what: Client and server side JavaScript framework for real time apps, with the Racer sync engine
competitors.traction_then: older than Meteor but fewer contributors
competitors.funding_then: stealth startup Lever behind it, amount not stated

competitors.name: Mojito
competitors.what: Yahoo Node.js framework bringing the MVC pattern to JavaScript apps

technical_complexity.rationale: A real time reactive full stack framework with a shared client and server model, and later a federated GraphQL gateway and client cache, are hard engineering problems for a small team.

defensibility.rationale: Large open source adoption and enterprise integrations create switching costs, but the core is open source and others can build compatible tools.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Large vendors did not absorb Meteor or Apollo. Meteor was sold in 2019 to Tiny Capital as the founders spun out to focus on Apollo. Apollo laid off roughly 15 percent in December 2022 per third party trackers.

market_need_then: In 2012 Meteor drew thousands of downloads within hours of a Hacker News post and raised 11.2 million dollars from a major VC that summer, showing developer demand for real time JavaScript frameworks.

branding.name_origin: Meteor Development Group's late 2015 project to rebuild the data layer was called the Apollo project; the team later renamed the company Apollo. The source does not explain why the name was chosen.
branding.domain_note: Uses apollographql.com. Not an exact brand match, which suggests the plain domain was not available.

identity.logo: space themed identity, details not confirmed
identity.visual_style: futuristic retro space look in a 2024 Basement Studio rebrand case study

branding.brand_signature: Space and rocket themed Apollo brand, inferred from a design agency case study titled A Brand Built for Liftoff
branding.community_and_virality: Large open source community, with the company claiming tens of millions of monthly downloads of its client, server and gateway. Active forum at community.apollographql.com.

brand_strength.rationale: Apollo Client became a default name in GraphQL, with a developer community and Fortune 500 use claimed on the YC page. Rating rests on company claims and community presence, not an independent brand study.

pivots.from: Meteor, a full stack JavaScript framework
pivots.to: Apollo, open source and commercial GraphQL data tooling
pivots.why: The team built a new data layer in late 2015 and chose GraphQL as a database agnostic query language; MDG released the Apollo stack in 2016 and sold Meteor in 2019 to focus on it

outcome_analysis: Apollo began as Meteor, raised 11.2 million dollars in 2012, then pivoted to GraphQL tooling that spread through open source adoption. It raised 22 million dollars in 2019 and 130 million at a reported valuation above 1.5 billion in 2021, then cut about 15 percent of staff in late 2022 as the funding climate cooled. It remains independent and active in 2026 selling a GraphOS platform to large enterprises.
notes: The 2012 round: TechCrunch gives 11.2 million dollars but names no investor in its text; Andreessen Horowitz is inferred from the URL slug of a linked story and is unconfirmed. It is labeled series_a because CB Insights lists a July 2012 Series A, which is an aggregator. A Series B in May 2015 appears on CB Insights without an amount (unverified, not recorded). The June 2019 round: Apollo's own post calls it Apollo's first venture capital round with no stage label, VentureBeat calls it a 22 million dollar Series C; recorded series_c per VentureBeat. VentureBeat says about 53 million raised before the Series D; CB Insights shows about 183 million total over eight rounds; not reconciled. Layoffs in December 2022 from a third party tracker, unverified. A YC page lists no bios for founders; PitchBook shows two small acquisitions (FathomDB 2014, Percolate Studio 2015) not recorded. The April Fools WunderGraph acquisition item is a joke and is ignored. Funding date for 2012 rounds, and the Meteor Development Group to Apollo rename date, are not stated in sources opened.
